title: 1% EXPENSE RATIO: 6 THINGS TO KNOW
series_label: 1% EXPENSE RATIO OVER 30 YEARS: 6 THINGS TO KNOW

concepts.title: The $18,050 Hit
concepts.body: A 1% expense ratio on $10,000 held 30 years costs you roughly $18,050 in lost growth (hypothetical, 7% gross). The fee itself is small per year — about $100 on $10,000 — but the compounding penalty is what hurts. That's the $18,050 number.

visual_spec.callout_text: 1% on $10K for 30 years = ~$100/yr in fees — but ~$18,050 in lost compounding at 7% gross. The fee you don't see is the fee that hurts most.

concepts.title: Scale It Up: $100K
concepts.body: Bump the starting balance to $100,000 and the math scales linearly. 1% on $100K for 30 years = ~$180,500 in lost growth. The percentage fee is the same; the dollar damage grows with the balance. This is why fees matter more as you accumulate.

concepts.title: What Counts As '1%'?
concepts.body: An expense ratio is the annual fee a fund charges, expressed as a % of your balance. 1% means $10 per year for every $1,000 invested. It's deducted automatically — you never see a bill. Low-cost index funds run 0.03% to 0.15%. Anything above 0.50% is expensive.

concepts.title: Real Fund Fees In 2026
concepts.body: Concretely: VOO is 0.03%, FXAIX 0.015%, VTI 0.03%, and a target date index like VTTSX is 0.08%. Many actively managed mutual funds run 0.60% to 1.00% or more. The gap between the cheapest and the priciest S&P 500 funds is 30x.

concepts.title: Gross Vs Net Return
concepts.body: Gross return is before fees; net is what lands in your account. The expense ratio is the automatic bridge between them. A fund with 7% gross and 0.50% fees returns 6.50% net — and that 0.50% gap compounds for decades, which is why the math above is so punitive.

visual_spec.callout_text: Gross return – expense ratio = net return. A 0.50% fee on 7% gross = 6.50% net. Small difference; big compounding consequence.

concepts.title: How To Audit Yours
concepts.body: Look up any fund's expense ratio on its fact sheet or your brokerage's fund page. Compare to the cheap index alternative for the same exposure. If the active fund costs 0.75% and the index costs 0.04%, you're paying 0.71% a year for stock-picking that — over 30 years — usually loses to the index.

right_points: Paying 1%+ for an index you can get for 0.03%

sources_footer: Sourced from Vanguard VOO/VTI fact sheets, Fidelity FXAIX prospectus, FINRA Fund Analyzer, SEC investor.gov
